answers.1: The county is deciding its 2027 budget, meaning what Fulton County will spend next year on things like the jail, courts and libraries. The Fulton County Board of Commissioners decides. It has a chairman (Robert Pitts) and six district seats, and District 4 is vacant. First, a four-person Budget Commission (the county manager, the chief financial officer, Commissioner Bob Ellis and Vice Chair Khadijah Abdur-Rahman) has to propose a budget by Nov 15, 2026. That group can't adopt it. Only the full Board can, as is or with changes, by its second regular January meeting, expected Jan 20, 2027 (it could vote earlier). There's also a fight over who sits on that Budget Commission and over a 5% limit on departments asking for extra money.
answers.2: The page can't say. It says whether my 2027 county property tax changes 'isn't known yet' as of Nov 8, 2026, because the proposed budget isn't public yet. So no amount and no date. It does say property tax is the county's main source of money, and that in 2026 the Board's hearing on the tax rate came months after its budget vote. That makes me think my tax bill gets settled separately and later, but the page doesn't say when that happens for 2027 or how the budget turns into my bill. There are headings called 'Where the money comes from' and 'Decided now, and decided later', but no text showed under them.
answers.3: Mostly property owners' money, since the page says property tax is the county's main income. It goes to county services: the jail, courts, libraries and others. Six of the justice offices (I think the sheriff, district attorney, solicitor-general, court clerk, probate judge and public defender) have asked for more money, citing staffing shortages, court delays and jail overcrowding. Departments' requests for extra money are capped at 5%, but the page never says 5% of what. The Board can add, cut or move money before it votes. There are no dollar amounts anywhere, not even the total budget. 'The county's savings' and 'the jail agreement' come up but aren't explained.
answers.4: Speak during public comment at a Board of Commissioners meeting, in person or by Zoom. The listed meetings are Nov 18, Dec 2 and Dec 16, 2026, at 10 a.m., at the Fulton County Government Center in Atlanta (January meetings are proposed for Jan 6 and Jan 20). Zoom comments and requests to speak in person must be in before 10 a.m., but the page says the Clerk's website doesn't say where to send them, so I'd call the Clerk to the Commission at 404-612-8200. That's also the number for asking how to send a written comment or for a disability accommodation. Each speaker gets up to 2 minutes, and Fulton residents go first. I can also watch the Clerk's Public Notices page for the budget public hearing (no date yet), look up my commissioner with the county's District Finder (District 4 is vacant, so people there contact the chairman), and read the proposal after Nov 15. The page gives no direct phone or email for any commissioner, and doesn't say where I'd find the proposal. By when: before the Board votes, which must be by its second regular January meeting, expected Jan 20, 2027. It could be earlier.
answers.5: 'Mixed' isn't used anywhere on this page. 'Uncertain' is one of the evidence labels on the argument cards, and the page says it means 'Nothing we found settles it yet.' The other labels are 'Supported' (the records back it up) and 'Values question' (about what's fair, which facts can't settle). But every card lists all three labels under 'Evidence:', so I couldn't tell which one applies to which card.
answers.6: For: 'The commission adds early input, and the full Board still decides.' North and south Fulton each get a commissioner shaping the draft, and the full Board still votes. Against: 'Two commissioners, seated under rules they sponsored, have too much say.' Department heads have to present their needs to just two commissioners instead of the full Board, and Commissioner Barrett says the rules let only those two serve.

seemed_to_favor: Mostly it felt even-handed. It says more than once that it doesn't recommend an option, labels its own analysis, and admits its gaps. But the critics of the current process came through louder. The page itself says its sources quote three critics (the probate judge, the sheriff and Commissioner Barrett) plus the solicitor-general on funding, against one supporter (Commissioner Ellis). The only 'in their own words' quote on the Options tab is from Barrett, the side that wanted to remove the 5% limit. Of the six argument cards, two back the current process, two criticize it, and two carry the justice officials' asks (wait until January, more money), with no card arguing against more justice money. The card title 'Two commissioners, seated under rules they sponsored, have too much say' also read a little pointed to me. The Board majority that voted to set aside the cap removal never explains itself, though the page says that's because no reasons are on record. I didn't feel told what to think, but the critics got more of the airtime.
hardest: Question 3 was hardest: the page never gives a single dollar amount, never says what the 5% limit is 5% of, and the 'Where the money comes from' section showed only a heading, so all I could say is 'mostly property tax, going to county services.' Question 2 was close behind, because the page hints the tax rate is set separately and months after the budget vote but never says when that happens for 2027.
